subject: how a person decides which clinic or hospital to use, and when they go past the nearest one
citation: Majola TN et al. (2026). Healthcare workers' perspectives on patient bypassing of Primary Health Care facilities in Mpumalanga province, South Africa. African Journal of Primary Health Care & Family Medicine. doi:10.4102/phcfm.v18i1.5368
Chavalala L et al. (2025). General Male Patients' Experiences When Visiting Public Health Facilities in Limpopo Province, South Africa. Public Health Challenges. doi:10.1002/puh2.70166

claims.text: Unfamiliarity with the referral system makes clinic-first entry read as optional, because patients do not know the correct starting point and go straight to casualty or hospital.

readings.text: Someone who brings a child straight to casualty without starting at the clinic would weigh a new referral policy mainly by whether it makes the correct starting point obvious before they travel.
If patients seek care wherever they want without understanding the system, they would treat a new service as one more place they may or may not choose to enter, not as a required step.

Someone who sees a lack of awareness as the reason patients bypass the clinic would be more open to a new product only if it visibly teaches the entry order, but would not assume people will follow it on their own.
If young mothers are among those who do not know the system, a new policy aimed at clinic-first entry would be weighed by whether it reaches them early enough to change where they first seek care.

claims.text: Negative experience of clinics as slow, under-resourced, and staffed by rude workers makes clinic-first rules read as burdensome, because patients judge the clinic as not worth following.
evaluative_rules: Judge a facility by whether it wastes your time, not by the official pathway.
Judge a facility by whether staff treat you like a human being.
objections: Will this waste my time like the clinic does?
Will the staff treat me like a human being?

readings.text: Someone who judges the clinic as not worth following because of long queues and slow service would weigh any new clinic-first rule as another delay to avoid, unless the rule clearly shortens waiting time.
If a person has experienced staff attitude in the clinic as rude and dehumanising, they would weigh a new clinic-first rule as forcing them back into mistreatment, making them less open to it.

Someone who believes clinics lack equipment, consulting rooms and drugs would weigh a new clinic-first rule as sending them to a place that cannot help them, so they would see little reason to follow it.

If a patient feels doctors treat them better than nurses and that hospitals offer quicker x-rays, they would weigh a new clinic-first rule as blocking access to better care, unless the clinic could offer the same examinations.

claims.text: Local clinics staffed by known community members with shared consulting rooms make locally delivered care read as exposing, because patients fear stigma and loss of confidentiality.
evaluative_rules: Judge a facility by whether your neighbours can see or learn your condition.
objections: Will people in my community see me or learn my condition?

readings.text: Someone who fears neighbours will make stigmatising comments about chronic diseases would weigh any new local service by whether it makes their attendance visible to people from the community.
If a person worries that community members work at the same local clinic, they would be cautious about a new service that draws on locally known staff.
Someone who avoids local clinics because of sensitive issues they would not want other people to know would look for clear separation from known staff in any new local offering.
If a person believes infrastructure limits confidentiality when health workers share consulting rooms, they would weigh a new service by whether it avoids shared spaces.

claims.text: Public facilities read as unwelcoming and unsafe for men, because male patients experience long waits, gender-biased triage, and humiliating treatment by female nurses.
evaluative_rules: Judge a facility by whether it welcomes men rather than prioritising women.

readings.text: Someone who has waited long hours without being told why would weigh a new service on whether it gives a clear reason for any delay and a place to sit while waiting.
Someone who has seen women helped quickly while he was left in the queue would weigh a new service on whether men are seen in the same order as women.
Someone who has had a female nurse joke about his condition to other patients would weigh a new service on whether consultations stay between him and the nurse.
Someone who found it difficult to open up to female nurses would weigh a new service on whether he can be helped by male staff.

claims.text: Clinic-based nurse interaction reads as threatening, because patients expect mistreatment from nurses based on experienced or reported harsh and disrespectful behaviour.
evaluative_rules: Judge a facility by whether nurses will keep your condition private and speak to you respectfully.
objections: Will I be humiliated or shouted at by nurses?

readings.text: Someone who expects nurses to joke about their condition to other patients would weigh any new clinic-based service by whether it limits what nurses can say to others about them.
If a person has been shouted at by a nurse for their condition, they would look at a new service for whether it reduces the chance of being spoken to harshly.
Someone who believes nurses should be trained to treat patients well and equally would judge a new service by whether it shows nurses being patient with people who are sick.
If a person has avoided facilities to escape victimisation by health workers, they would weigh a new service by whether it keeps them away from direct nurse interaction.

region: Mpumalanga and Limpopo provinces, South Africa
confidence: Two qualitative studies: 20 healthcare workers at 10 Mpumalanga hospitals (so the bypassing reasons are staff-reported, not patients' own words) and 28 men in four focus groups in Limpopo. Fieldwork dates are not stated in either paper; the years shown are publication years. Mechanisms durable; magnitudes unknown.
